        -: 1248: *              hash without knowing its plaintext version at all.

        -: 1174:
        -: 1175:/* Replication buffer blocks is the list of replBufBlock.
        -: 1176: *
        -: 1177: * +--------------+       +--------------+       +--------------+
        -: 1178: * | refcount = 1 |  ...  | refcount = 0 |  ...  | refcount = 2 |
        -: 1179: * +--------------+       +--------------+       +--------------+
        -: 1180: *      |                                            /       \
        -: 1181: *      |                                           /         \
        -: 1182: *      |                                          /           \
        -: 1183: *  Repl Backlog                               Replica_A    Replica_B
        -: 1184: *
        -: 1185: * Each replica or replication backlog increments only the refcount of the
        -: 1186: * 'ref_repl_buf_node' which it points to. So when replica walks to the next
        -: 1187: * node, it should first increase the next node's refcount, and when we trim
        -: 1188: * the replication buffer nodes, we remove node always from the head node which
        -: 1189: * refcount is 0. If the refcount of the head node is not 0, we must stop
        -: 1190: * trimming and never iterate the next node.
        -: 1191: *
        -: 1192: * For replicas in IO threads we don't update the refcount while sending the
        -: 1193: * repl data, but only when the client is sent back to main. This avoids data
        -: 1194: * races. In order to achieve this, the replicas keep track of following:
        -: 1195: * - io_curr_repl_node - the current node we've reached.
        -: 1196: * - io_bound_repl_node - the last node in the replication buffer as seen by
        -: 1197: *                        the replica client before it was sent to IO thread
        -: 1198: *
        -: 1199: * When the client is sent to IO thread for the first time io_curr_repl_node is
        -: 1200: * initialized with ref_repl_buf_node.
        -: 1201: * When the client is sent back to main it can decrement ref_repl_buf_node's
        -: 1202: * refcount and increment it for io_curr_repl_node, since all the nodes
        -: 1203: * in-between are already sent and the client doesn't hold reference to them.
        -: 1204: *
        -: 1205: * `io_bound_repl_node` is needed because IO thread needs to know when to stop

        -: 2961:
        -: 2962:/* Redis command structure.
        -: 2963: *
        -: 2964: * Note that the command table is in commands.c and it is auto-generated.
        -: 2965: *
        -: 2966: * This is the meaning of the flags:
        -: 2967: *
        -: 2968: * CMD_WRITE:       Write command (may modify the key space).
        -: 2969: *
        -: 2970: * CMD_READONLY:    Commands just reading from keys without changing the content.
        -: 2971: *                  Note that commands that don't read from the keyspace such as
        -: 2972: *                  TIME, SELECT, INFO, administrative commands, and connection
        -: 2973: *                  or transaction related commands (multi, exec, discard, ...)
        -: 2974: *                  are not flagged as read-only commands, since they affect the
        -: 2975: *                  server or the connection in other ways.
        -: 2976: *
        -: 2977: * CMD_DENYOOM:     May increase memory usage once called. Don't allow if out
        -: 2978: *                  of memory.
        -: 2979: *
        -: 2980: * CMD_ADMIN:       Administrative command, like SAVE or SHUTDOWN.
        -: 2981: *
        -: 2982: * CMD_PUBSUB:      Pub/Sub related command.
        -: 2983: *
        -: 2984: * CMD_NOSCRIPT:    Command not allowed in scripts.
        -: 2985: *
        -: 2986: * CMD_BLOCKING:    The command has the potential to block the client.
        -: 2987: *
        -: 2988: * CMD_LOADING:     Allow the command while loading the database.
        -: 2989: *
        -: 2990: * CMD_NO_ASYNC_LOADING: Deny during async loading (when a replica uses diskless
        -: 2991: *                       sync swapdb, and allows access to the old dataset)
        -: 2992: *
        -: 2993: * CMD_STALE:       Allow the command while a slave has stale data but is not
        -: 2994: *                  allowed to serve this data. Normally no command is accepted
        -: 2995: *                  in this condition but just a few.
        -: 2996: *
        -: 2997: * CMD_SKIP_MONITOR:  Do not automatically propagate the command on MONITOR.
        -: 2998: *
        -: 2999: * CMD_SKIP_SLOWLOG:  Do not automatically propagate the command to the slowlog.
        -: 3000: *
        -: 3001: * CMD_ASKING:      Perform an implicit ASKING for this command, so the
        -: 3002: *                  command will be accepted in cluster mode if the slot is marked
        -: 3003: *                  as 'importing'.
        -: 3004: *
        -: 3005: * CMD_FAST:        Fast command: O(1) or O(log(N)) command that should never
        -: 3006: *                  delay its execution as long as the kernel scheduler is giving
        -: 3007: *                  us time. Note that commands that may trigger a DEL as a side
        -: 3008: *                  effect (like SET) are not fast commands.
        -: 3009: *
        -: 3010: * CMD_NO_AUTH:     Command doesn't require authentication
        -: 3011: *
        -: 3012: * CMD_MAY_REPLICATE:   Command may produce replication traffic, but should be
        -: 3013: *                      allowed under circumstances where write commands are disallowed.
        -: 3014: *                      Examples include PUBLISH, which replicates pubsub messages,and
        -: 3015: *                      EVAL, which may execute write commands, which are replicated,
        -: 3016: *                      or may just execute read commands. A command can not be marked
        -: 3017: *                      both CMD_WRITE and CMD_MAY_REPLICATE
        -: 3018: *
        -: 3019: * CMD_SENTINEL:    This command is present in sentinel mode.
        -: 3020: *
        -: 3021: * CMD_ONLY_SENTINEL: This command is present only when in sentinel mode.
        -: 3022: *                    And should be removed from redis.
        -: 3023: *
        -: 3024: * CMD_NO_MANDATORY_KEYS: This key arguments for this command are optional.
        -: 3025: *
        -: 3026: * CMD_NO_MULTI: The command is not allowed inside a transaction
        -: 3027: *
        -: 3028: * CMD_ALLOW_BUSY: The command can run while another command is running for
        -: 3029: *                 a long time (timedout script, module command that yields)
        -: 3030: *
        -: 3031: * CMD_TOUCHES_ARBITRARY_KEYS: The command may touch (and cause lazy-expire)
        -: 3032: *                             arbitrary key (i.e not provided in argv)
        -: 3033: *
        -: 3034: * CMD_INTERNAL: The command may perform operations without performing
        -: 3035: *               validations such as ACL.
        -: 3036: *
        -: 3037: * The following additional flags are only used in order to put commands
        -: 3038: * in a specific ACL category. Commands can have multiple ACL categories.
        -: 3039: * See redis.conf for the exact meaning of each.
        -: 3040: *

        -:  260: * reflect the same time.

       17:  262:mstime_t commandTimeSnapshot(void) {
        -:  263:    /* When we are in the middle of a command execution, we want to use a
        -:  264:     * reference time that does not change: in that case we just use the
        -:  265:     * cached time, that we update before each call in the call() function.
        -:  266:     * This way we avoid that commands such as RPOPLPUSH or similar, that
        -:  267:     * may re-open the same key multiple times, can invalidate an already
        -:  268:     * open object in a next call, if the next call will see the key expired,
        -:  269:     * while the first did not.
        -:  270:     * This is specifically important in the context of scripts, where we
        -:  271:     * pretend that time freezes. This way a key can expire only the first time

        -: 3354: *    the key at index 2 was added before the spec of the key at
        -: 3355: *    index 1).

        -: 3357: *

        -:  228:/* API for alternative cluster implementations to start and coordinate
        -:  229: * Atomic Slot Migration (ASM).
        -:  230: *
        -:  231: * These two functions drive ASM for alternative cluster implementations.
        -:  232: * - clusterAsmProcess(...) impl -> redis: initiates/advances/cancels ASM operations
        -:  233: * - clusterAsmOnEvent(...) redis -> impl: notifies state changes
        -:  234: *
        -:  235: * Generic steps for an alternative implementation:
        -:  236: * - On destination side, implementation calls clusterAsmProcess(ASM_EVENT_IMPORT_START)
        -:  237: *   to start an import operation.
        -:  238: * - Redis calls clusterAsmOnEvent() when an ASM event occurs.
        -:  239: * - On the source side, Redis will call clusterAsmOnEvent(ASM_EVENT_HANDOFF_PREP)
        -:  240: *   when slots are ready to be handed off and the write pause is needed.
        -:  241: * - Implementation stops the traffic to the slots and calls clusterAsmProcess(ASM_EVENT_HANDOFF)
        -:  242: * - On the destination side, Redis calls clusterAsmOnEvent(ASM_EVENT_TAKEOVER)
        -:  243: *   when destination node is ready to take over the slot, waiting for ownership change.
        -:  244: * - Cluster implementation updates the config and calls clusterAsmProcess(ASM_EVENT_DONE)
        -:  245: *   to notify Redis that the slots ownership has changed.
        -:  246: *
        -:  247: * Sequence diagram for import:
        -:  248: *   - Note: shows only the events that cluster implementation needs to react.
        -:  249: *
        -:  250: * ┌───────────────┐              ┌───────────────┐         ┌───────────────┐             ┌───────────────┐
        -:  251: * │ Destination   │              │ Destination   │         │    Source     │             │ Source        │
        -:  252: * │ Cluster impl  │              │ Master        │         │    Master     │             │ Cluster impl  │
        -:  253: * └───────┬───────┘              └───────┬───────┘         └───────┬───────┘             └───────┬───────┘
        -:  254: *         │                              │                         │                             │
        -:  255: *         │     ASM_EVENT_IMPORT_START   │                         │                             │
        -:  256: *         ├─────────────────────────────►│                         │                             │
        -:  257: *         │                              │ CLUSTER SYNCSLOTS <arg> │                             │
        -:  258: *         │                              ├────────────────────────►│                             │
        -:  259: *         │                              │                         │                             │
        -:  260: *         │                              │  SNAPSHOT(restore cmds) │                             │
        -:  261: *         │                              │◄────────────────────────┤                             │
        -:  262: *         │                              │  Repl stream            │                             │
        -:  263: *         │                              │◄────────────────────────┤                             │
        -:  264: *         │                              │                         │   ASM_EVENT_HANDOFF_PREP    │
        -:  265: *         │                              │                         ├────────────────────────────►│
        -:  266: *         │                              │                         │     ASM_EVENT_HANDOFF       │
        -:  267: *         │                              │                         │◄────────────────────────────┤
        -:  268: *         │                              │ Drain repl stream       │                             │
        -:  269: *         │                              │◄────────────────────────┤                             │
        -:  270: *         │     ASM_EVENT_TAKEOVER       │                         │                             │
        -:  271: *         │◄─────────────────────────────┤                         │                             │
        -:  272: *         │                              │                         │                             │
        -:  273: *         │       ASM_EVENT_DONE         │                         │                             │
        -:  274: *         ├─────────────────────────────►│                         │       ASM_EVENT_DONE        │
        -:  275: *         │                              │                         │◄────────────────────────────┤
        -:  276: *         │                              │                         │                             │
        -:  277: */
        -:  278:
        -:  279:#define ASM_EVENT_IMPORT_START      1  /* Start a new import operation (destination side) */
        -:  280:#define ASM_EVENT_CANCEL            2  /* Cancel an ongoing import/migrate operation (source and destination side) */
        -:  281:#define ASM_EVENT_HANDOFF_PREP      3  /* Slot is ready to be handed off to the destination shard (source side) */
        -:  282:#define ASM_EVENT_HANDOFF           4  /* Notify that the slot can be handed off (source side) */
        -:  283:#define ASM_EVENT_TAKEOVER          5  /* Ready to take over the slot, waiting for config change (destination side) */
        -:  284:#define ASM_EVENT_DONE              6  /* Notify that import/migrate is completed, config is updated (source and destination side) */
        -:  285:
        -:  286:#define ASM_EVENT_IMPORT_PREP       7  /* Import is about to start, the implementation may reject by returning C_ERR */
        -:  287:#define ASM_EVENT_IMPORT_STARTED    8  /* Import started */
        -:  288:#define ASM_EVENT_IMPORT_FAILED     9  /* Import failed */
        -:  289:#define ASM_EVENT_IMPORT_COMPLETED  10 /* Import completed (config updated) */
        -:  290:#define ASM_EVENT_MIGRATE_PREP      11 /* Migrate is about to start, the implementation may reject by returning C_ERR */
        -:  291:#define ASM_EVENT_MIGRATE_STARTED   12 /* Migrate started */
        -:  292:#define ASM_EVENT_MIGRATE_FAILED    13 /* Migrate failed */

        -:  302: *

        -:  304: * For other events (ASM_EVENT_CANCEL, ASM_EVENT_HANDOFF, ASM_EVENT_DONE),
        -:  305: * 'task_id' should match the ID from the corresponding import operation.
        -:  306: *    Usage:
        -:  307: *      char *task_id = malloc(CLUSTER_NAMELEN + 1);

        -:  329: *  - Returns C_OK on success, C_ERR on failure and 'err' will be set to the
        -:  330: *    error message.

        -:  332: * Memory management:
        -:  333: *  - There is no ownership transfer of 'task_id', 'err' or `slotRangeArray`.

        -:  335: *     caller. Redis internally will make a copy of these.

        -:  269:/*-----------------------------------------------------------------------------
        -:  270: * Hash template registry internals
        -:  271: *
        -:  272: * Many hashes often share the exact same set of field names (e.g. rows of one
        -:  273: * "schema"). Instead of repeating the field names in every key, a single
        -:  274: * immutable template stores the names once and every matching hash references
        -:  275: * it, keeping only its own values. This is a memory optimization aimed at large
        -:  276: * populations of hashes with a stable, identical field set.
        -:  277: *
        -:  278: * A template is identified by its exact set of field names and is never
        -:  279: * changed once created. So adding a field (HSET) or removing one (HDEL) does
        -:  280: * not edit the template: the hash just switches to the template for the new
        -:  281: * field set, reusing it if it already exists or creating it otherwise (see
        -:  282: * hashTemplateGetOrCreateWithHash). This makes changing the field set more
        -:  283: * costly than on a plain hash, so the feature is meant for many hashes that
        -:  284: * keep the same fields mostly stable.
        -:  285: *
        -:  286: * Fields are kept sorted inside the template by sdscmplen (length, then bytes;
        -:  287: * see hashTemplateValidateFields). A field lookup binary-searches the sorted
        -:  288: * names for its index (hashTemplateFieldIndex), then reads the value stored at
        -:  289: * that same index.
        -:  290: *
        -:  291: * Two value encodings reference a template:
        -:  292: *   OBJ_ENCODING_TMPL_LP    - o->ptr is a listpack laid out as
        -:  293: *                             [template_id (varint)][v0][v1]...[vN-1]. Values
        -:  294: *                             are packed inline and the leading id maps back to
        -:  295: *                             the template. Compact, used for small hashes.
        -:  296: *                             Lookup: lpSeek(lp, idx + 1) (the +1 skips the id).
        -:  297: *   OBJ_ENCODING_TMPL_ARRAY - o->ptr is a hashTemplateArray { tmpl_id; sds
        -:  298: *                             values[] } holding the values in template field
        -:  299: *                             order. Used once listpack limits are exceeded (or
        -:  300: *                             there are many fields). Lookup: values[idx].
        -:  301: *
        -:  302: * Registry: htemplates->by_fields maps a sorted field set to its template, and
        -:  303: * htemplates->by_id maps a small integer id to the template. TMPL_LP stores
        -:  304: * this id inline rather than an 8-byte pointer, so a key's reference to its
        -:  305: * template can be as little as ~2 bytes. RDB save uses it the same way: each
        -:  306: * template is written once and every key just references it by this id.
        -:  307: *
        -:  308: * Lifetime and threading: each referencing key holds a key_refcount to its
        -:  309: * template and a client can also hold a hold_refcount (e.g. a fieldset
        -:  310: * registered with HIMPORT PREPARE). A single template may back a huge number of
        -:  311: * keys and those keys are often freed in bulk in the background by a BIO
        -:  312: * lazyfree thread (e.g. background trim after ASM). The registry is main thread
        -:  313: * only, so a BIO thread must not touch it: instead the BIO lazyfree thread records
        -:  314: * per-template key drop counts and publishes them to the main thread, which 
        -:  315: * applies the drops and frees any template reaching zero refs in cron (see bio_pending_drops).
        -:  316: *----------------------------------------------------------------------------*/

        -: 3153:
        -: 3154:/* ------------------------------------------------------------------------- *
        -: 3155: * RDB-load automatic template conversion
        -: 3156: *
        -: 3157: * Background: a template holds one shared copy of a hash's field names, so many
        -: 3158: * hashes with the same fields can drop their per-key field-name copies and point
        -: 3159: * at the template instead. This only pays off when a template is shared by many
        -: 3160: * keys; a template used by a single key costs more memory than it saves.
        -: 3161: *
        -: 3162: * While loading a whole RDB we can opportunistically turn plain hashes into
        -: 3163: * template-based ones. Three configs control this. They apply to RDB load
        -: 3164: * only (not to RESTORE/DUMP), and all of them are skipped if the RDB already
        -: 3165: * carries a template header:
        -: 3166: *
        -: 3167: *   - hash-rdb-load-min-template-entries: min field count for a hash to be
        -: 3168: *     eligible (0 = feature off, nothing is converted).
        -: 3169: *   - hash-rdb-load-max-template-entries: max field count (0 = no upper bound).
        -: 3170: *   - hash-rdb-load-template-disassembly-threshold: how many keys a template
        -: 3171: *     must have to be worth keeping (0 = this context off; every eligible hash is
        -: 3172: *     converted and kept).
        -: 3173: *
        -: 3174: * Goal: keep templates that are shared by many keys and avoid templates that end
        -: 3175: * up with only a few keys: such a template wastes memory instead of saving it.
        -: 3176: * We call a template "few-key" while its key count is below the threshold.
        -: 3177: *
        -: 3178: * The context does two things during the load:
        -: 3179: *   - Throttle: once few-key templates clearly dominate, stop creating new
        -: 3180: *     templates (hashes whose fields match an existing template still attach).
        -: 3181: *   - Disassemble: at end of load, turn every template still below the threshold
        -: 3182: *     key count back into a plain LISTPACK/HT hash.

        -:    6:/*
        -:    7: * Simple append-only vector (dynamic array) of void * elements.
        -:    8: *
        -:    9: * Design:
        -:   10: * --------
        -:   11: * - Stores elements in a contiguous array (void **).
        -:   12: * - Supports append (vecPush) and read access.
        -:   13: * - Optionally uses caller-provided stack buffer to avoid heap allocations.
        -:   14: * - See also comment in vector.c of vecInit() for more details.
        -:   15: *
        -:   16: * Memory:
        -:   17: * -------
        -:   18: * - vecRelease() frees heap memory if used.
        -:   19: * - Stack buffer is never freed.
        -:   20: * - Stored elements are never freed.
        -:   21: *
        -:   22: * Modes:
        -:   23: * ------- 
        -:   24: * 1. Start On Stack (grow to heap): vec v;
        -:   25: *                                   void *vstack[8];
        -:   26: *                                   ...
        -:   27: *                                   vecInit(&v, vstack, 8);
        -:   28: *
        -:   29: *   Start Embedded (grow to heap):  typedef struct { 
        -:   30: *                                     vec v; 
        -:   31: *                                     void *vembedded[8]; 
        -:   32: *                                   } obj;
        -:   33: *                                   ...
        -:   34: *                                   vecInit(&obj->v, obj->vembedded, 8);
        -:   35: *
        -:   36: * 2. Heap only, init capacity 8:    vec v;
        -:   37: *                                   ...
        -:   38: *                                   vecInit(&v, NULL, 8);
        -:   39: *
        -:   40: *    Heap only, init capacity 0:    vec v;
        -:   41: *                                   ...
        -:   42: *                                   vecInit(&v, NULL, 0);
        -:   43: *
        -:   44: * 3. Depends on var size:           vec v;
        -:   45: *                                   void *vstack[8];
        -:   46: *                                   vecInit(&v, vstack, 8);
        -:   47: *                                   vecReserve(&v, varsize); // varsize <= 8 ? stack : heap
        -:   48: *
        -:   49: * Notes:
        -:   50: * ------
        -:   51: * - Not thread-safe.
        -:   52: * - If stack == NULL and initcap > 0, initcap is treated as an initial
        -:   53: *   heap-capacity hint.
        -:   54: * - When used in Redis core, the implementation should use the Redis allocator
        -:   55: *   wrappers (zmalloc / zrealloc / zfree) rather than libc allocation APIs.
        -:   56: */
        -:   57:

        -:   29: *     +---------+------------+----------------------------+

        -:   32: *
        -:   33: *

        -:   35: *     With this type, both the key and value are embedded.  Extra bits in the 
        -:   36: *     sdshdr8 (on field) are used to encode aux flags which may indicate the 
        -:   37: *     presence of an optional expiration. Extra padding is included in the value 
        -:   38: *     to the size of the physical block.
        -:   39: *
        -:   40: *                            entry

        -:   45: *     +--------------+---------+------------+----------------------------+

        -:   48: *

        -:    1:/*
        -:    2: * Copyright Redis Ltd. 2024 - present
        -:    3: *
        -:    4: * Licensed under your choice of (a) the Redis Source Available License 2.0
        -:    5: * (RSALv2); or (b) the Server Side Public License v1 (SSPLv1); or (c) the
        -:    6: * GNU Affero General Public License v3 (AGPLv3).
        -:    7: *
        -:    8: *
        -:    9: * WHAT IS EBUCKETS?
        -:   10: * -----------------
        -:   11: * ebuckets is being used to store items that are set with expiration-time. It
        -:   12: * supports the basic API of add, remove and active expiration. The implementation
        -:   13: * of it is based on rax-tree, or plain linked-list when small. The expiration time
        -:   14: * of the items are used as the key to traverse rax-tree.
        -:   15: *
        -:   16: * Instead of holding a distinct item in each leaf of the rax-tree we can aggregate
        -:   17: * items into small segments and hold it in each leaf. This way we can  avoid
        -:   18: * frequent modification of the rax-tree, since many of the modifications
        -:   19: * will be done only at the segment level. It will also save memory because
        -:   20: * rax-tree can be costly, around 40 bytes per leaf (with rax-key limited to 6
        -:   21: * bytes). Whereas each additional item in the segment will cost the size of the
        -:   22: * 'next' pointer in a list (8 bytes) and few more bytes for maintenance of the
        -:   23: * segment.
        -:   24: *
        -:   25: * EBUCKETS STRUCTURE
        -:   26: * ------------------
        -:   27: * The ebuckets data structure is organized in a hierarchical manner as follows:
        -:   28: *
        -:   29: * 1. ebuckets: This is the top-level data structure. It can be either a rax tree
        -:   30: *    or a plain linked list. It contains one or more buckets, each representing
        -:   31: *    an interval in time.
        -:   32: *
        -:   33: * 2. bucket: Each bucket represents an interval in time and contains one or more
        -:   34: *    segments. The key in the rax-tree for each bucket represents low
        -:   35: *    bound expiration-time for the items within this bucket. The key of the
        -:   36: *    following bucket represents the upper bound expiration-time.
        -:   37: *
        -:   38: * 3. segment: Each segment within a bucket can hold up to `EB_SEG_MAX_ITEMS`
        -:   39: *    items as a linked list. If there are more, the segment will try to
        -:   40: *    split the bucket. To avoid wasting memory, it is a singly linked list (only
        -:   41: *    next-item pointer). It is a cyclic linked-list to allow efficient removal of
        -:   42: *    items from the middle of the segment without traversing the rax tree.
        -:   43: *
        -:   44: * 4. item: Each item that is stored in ebuckets should embed the ExpireMeta
        -:   45: *    struct and supply getter function (see EbucketsType.getExpireMeta). This
        -:   46: *    struct holds the expire-time of the item and few more fields that are used
        -:   47: *    to maintain the segments data-structure.
        -:   48: *
        -:   49: * SPLITTING BUCKET
        -:   50: * ----------------
        -:   51: * Each segment can hold up-to `EB_SEG_MAX_ITEMS` items. On insertion of new
        -:   52: * item, it will try to split the segment. Here is an example For adding item
        -:   53: * with expiration of 42 to a segment that already reached its maximum capacity
        -:   54: * which will cause to split of the segment and in turn split of the bucket as
        -:   55: * well to a finer grained ranges:
        -:   56: *
        -:   57: *       BUCKETS                             BUCKETS
        -:   58: *      [ 00-10 ] -> size(Seg0) = 11   ==>  [ 00-10 ] -> size(Seg0) = 11
        -:   59: *      [ 11-76 ] -> size(Seg1) = 16        [ 11-36 ] -> size(Seg1) = 9
        -:   60: *                                          [ 37-76 ] -> size(Seg2) = 7
        -:   61: *
        -:   62: * EXTENDING BUCKET
        -:   63: * ----------------
        -:   64: * In the example above, the reason it wasn't split evenly is that Seg1 must have
        -:   65: * been holding items with same TTL and they must reside together in the same
        -:   66: * bucket after the split. Which brings us to another important point. If there
        -:   67: * is a segment that reached its maximum capacity and all the items have same
        -:   68: * expiration-time key, then we cannot split the bucket but aggregate all the
        -:   69: * items, with same expiration time key, by allocating an extended-segment and
        -:   70: * chain it to the first segment in visited bucket. In that sense, extended
        -:   71: * segments will only hold items with same expiration-time key.
        -:   72: *
        -:   73: *       BUCKETS                            BUCKETS
        -:   74: *      [ 00-10 ] -> size(Seg0)=11   ==>   [ 00-10 ] -> size(Seg0)=11
        -:   75: *      [ 11-12 ] -> size(Seg1)=16         [ 11-12 ] -> size(Seg1)=1 -> size(Seg2)=16
        -:   76: *
        -:   77: * LIMITING RAX TREE DEPTH
        -:   78: * -----------------------
        -:   79: * The rax tree is basically a B-tree and its depth is bounded by the sizeof of
        -:   80: * the key. Holding 6 bytes for expiration-time key is more than enough to represent
        -:   81: * unix-time in msec, and in turn the depth of the tree is limited to 6 levels.
        -:   82: * At a first glance it might look sufficient but we need take into consideration
        -:   83: * the heavyweight maintenance and traversal of each node in the B-tree.
        -:   84: *
        -:   85: * And so, we can further prune the tree such that holding keys with msec precision
        -:   86: * in the tree doesn't bring with it much value. The active-expiration operation can
        -:   87: * live with deletion of expired items, say, older than 1 sec, which means the size
        -:   88: * of time-expiration keys to the rax tree become no more than ~4.5 bytes and we
        -:   89: * also get rid of the "noisy" bits which most probably will cause to yet another
        -:   90: * branching and modification of the rax tree in case of items with time-expiration
        -:   91: * difference of less than 1 second. The lazy expiration will still be precise and
        -:   92: * without compromise on accuracy because the exact expiration-time is kept
        -:   93: * attached as well to each item, in `ExpireMeta`, and each traversal of item with
        -:   94: * expiration will behave as expected down to the msec. Take care to configure
        -:   95: * `EB_BUCKET_KEY_PRECISION` according to your needs.
        -:   96: *
        -:   97: * EBUCKET KEY
        -:   98: * -----------
        -:   99: * Taking into account configured value of `EB_BUCKET_KEY_PRECISION`, two items
        -:  100: * with expiration-time t1 and t2 will be considered to have the same key in the
        -:  101: * rax-tree/buckets if and only if:
        -:  102: *
        -:  103: *              EB_BUCKET_KEY(t1) == EB_BUCKET_KEY(t2)
        -:  104: *
        -:  105: * EBUCKETS CREATION
        -:  106: * -----------------
        -:  107: * To avoid the cost of allocating rax data-structure for only few elements,
        -:  108: * ebuckets will start as a simple linked-list and only when it reaches some
        -:  109: * threshold, it will be converted to rax.
        -:  110: *
        -:  111: * TODO
        -:  112: * ----
        -:  113: * - ebRemove() optimize to merge small segments into one segment.
        -:  114: * - ebAdd() Fix pathological case of cascade addition of items into rax such
        -:  115: *   that their values are smaller/bigger than visited extended-segment which ends
        -:  116: *   up with multiple segments with a single item in each segment.
        -:  117: */
        -:  118:
        -:  119:#ifndef __EBUCKETS_H
        -:  120:#define __EBUCKETS_H

        -:  130: * expiration-time when mapping to buckets. The higher the value, the more items
        -:  131: * with similar expiration-time will be aggregated into the same bucket. The lower
        -:  132: * the value, the more "accurate" the active expiration of buckets will be.
